title: Great Faith, Great Doubt, Great Determination
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the Zen teaching of great faith, great doubt, and great determination, reading Torei Zenji's Bodhisattva Vow and passages on faith from Kyogen Carlson. Nomon pauses after each paragraph of the vow and recalls a work day at Green Gulch when a man named Terry folded his jacket and called it Buddha's clothing. Kyogen's three levels of faith build toward the deepest, that it is okay no matter what happens, and Nomon adds Kyogen's advice that if zazen is in the middle of everything, it always works out. Great doubt gets a short gloss, "don't be so sure." Nomon ends with Chogyam Trungpa's line: "The bad news is we're all falling. The good news is there's no bottom."

sentences.text: We're starting the talk with a little chant too, in the book somewhere.
*Unsurpassed, penetrating, and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having yet to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Good Sunday morning, everybody.
It's a beautiful day here in Bellingham.
Of course, with the beauty, right, our hearts always feel, or maybe try to avoid, but can't help feeling the sadness in the world, and the joy in the world, and the beauty in the world.
Beautiful day here, and probably today in Ukraine, the neighborhood was leveled, you know.
So hard to hold it all, probably impossible.
But a few thoughts from the dharma can help.
So I want to talk a little bit about a core Zen teaching: that the path to wherever, the path to waking up, we could say, has three essential elements.
Before I say that, there are about a million different lists of essential elements, right?
This particular three is from Japanese Zen, probably a later edition, and it's the three elements of great faith, great doubt, and great determination.
It gets talked about a little bit more in Rinzai Zen than in our more gentle Soto school.
Critics might call us a little lazy, but that's all right.
Some years ago, Jeff Kelly, who used to be the teacher in Seattle, and I did a sesshin together focused on these three, and we gave talks on great faith, great doubt, and great determination.
One year I also did the annual calligraphy card with the characters for this.
Like all the teachings, it slips out of my mind for periods, and then it bubbles back up pretty regularly.
So there are some talks by Jeff and me on this.
Speaking of which, I'm happy to share that I'm working with Michael, who's our new part-time staff person, Michael Calbera, program administrator.
He's helping to organize the Dharma Talks so that we'll be able to find them, something many of you have asked for over the years.
It'll be findable by topic and by author, and it'll be a system that can keep itself up to date, too.
So that's great.
I'm happy about that, because we have such a treasure of all these Dharma Talks.
A lot of helpful and interesting and empowering stuff, or maybe at least entertaining.
You can listen at home, you can listen in the car, you can put on your headphones and listen while you go on a walk.
And here we are creating another one for our collection, so I want to thank you for helping with that.
Thank you for being here today to help create the context, the essential community, sangha context that brings these talks to life.
Because it really isn't just that one of us goes off and makes some notes and prepares something and then just blah, blah, blah, delivers it.
Dharma Talks really come alive in the context, the dynamic functioning of our practice together.
As I speak these words and you receive them, the way that I speak them and the way that you receive them is mutually created.
So I wouldn't speak the same way if you weren't there, and you wouldn't hear them either, I guess.
That makes sense.
Even if that involves some spacing out and nodding off or thinking about something else, it still works, so don't worry.
Sometimes I space out a little as I'm speaking, to be honest.
What was I saying?
It's just the mind.
So: great faith, great doubt, great determination.
I got a little curious where this teaching came from.
A lot of stuff is just passed down, you hear it said.
And that's wonderful.
It's wonderful just to receive these things and really practice with them and have some faith in them, the first of those three.
But it's also interesting, and respectful of the tradition, I think, to get curious about the history and the cultural context.
Even if sometimes there are apparent contradictions between what the tradition says and what the historians seem to say, we can still hold them both.
Just like the holding of this beautiful and tragic day.
So anyway, I looked it up and it appears that these three are attributed to an 18th century Japanese Zen monk named Torai Enji, Torai.
And he was a disciple of the very famous Hakuen, Hakuen Eikaku.
Hakuen, the teacher of this fellow, Torai, Torai, Torai, sorry, Torai Zenji.
Anyway, Hakuen, his teacher, is really important in the Rinzai school.
He's kind of like their Dogen, one for whom the big deal honorific Zenji is used, which means Zen master.
So when we're being formal, we might say Dogen Zenji and they would say Hakuen Zenji.
So here is Hakuen's student, Torai.
And you know that a teacher is important if their poem or their saying or their expression makes it into what we chant, makes it into the chant book, into the liturgy.
So we have two or three, four examples of that in our chant book: Dogen and a few Chinese masters.
And Torai Zenji made it into the Rinzai chant book with his wonderful vow called Torai Zenji's Bodhisattva vow.
So I want to share that with you because it does express these three ideas of great faith, great doubt and great determination.
Torai Zenji, hundreds of years ago, 18th century, said:
*I am only a simple disciple, but I offer these respectful words.
When I regard the true nature of the many dharmas, the many experiences, the many dharmas, I find them all to be sacred forms of the Tathagata's never failing essence.*
*Each particle of matter, each moment is no other than the Tathagata's inexpressible radiance.*
So, everything.
*And with this realization, our virtuous ancestors gave tender care to beasts and birds with compassionate minds and hearts.
Among us in our daily lives, who is not reverently grateful for the protections of life?
Who is not grateful for food, drink and clothing?
Though these are inanimate things, they are nonetheless the warm flesh and blood, the merciful incarnations of Buddha.
All the more we can be especially sympathetic and affectionate with foolish people, particularly with someone who becomes a sworn enemy and persecutes us with abusive language.

This very abuse conveys the Buddha's boundless loving-kindness and is a compassionate device to liberate us entirely from the mean-spirited delusions we have built up with our own wrongful conduct from the beginningless past.
With our open response to such abuse, we compare ourselves, and the most profound and pure faith arises.*
*At the peak of each thought, a lotus flower opens, and on each flower there is revealed a Buddha.
Everywhere in the Pure Land is its beauty.
We fully see the Tathagata's radiant light right where we are.
May we retain this mind and extend it throughout the world, so that we and all beings become mature in Buddha's wisdom.*
So, as always in Dharma stuff, there's a lot there.
Let's listen to that again.
Maybe I'll say a few words after each paragraph.
*I'm only a simple disciple, but I offer these respectful words.*
These teachers really mean that.
His Holiness the Dalai Lama always says that: I'm just a humble monk.
It's not just saying that.
This practice really does lead to humility.
What do we actually know?
But we also do have faith and an understanding, so then it goes on.
*When I regard the true nature of the many Dharmas, I find them all to be sacred forms of the Tathagata's never failing essence.
Each particle of matter, each moment, is no other than the Tathagata's inexpressible radiance.*
So, this is like a heart teaching, isn't it?
Zen has a reputation for being very stern and intense, and maybe that seems a little head-oriented, wisdom-oriented, but this is a heart teaching.
Everything is sacred, is radiant, is Buddha.
And then he thinks about the ancestors, those who came before us and held this understanding.
*With this realization, our virtuous ancestors,*
they understood this.
*They gave tender care to beasts and birds with compassionate minds and hearts.
Among us, in our own daily lives, who is not reverently grateful for the protections of life?
Food, drink, and clothing, though their inanimate things are nonetheless the warm flesh and blood, the merciful incarnations of Buddha.*
That always makes me think of one time when I was young, man, at Green Gulch.
We were doing a work project, me and a couple other people, and this fellow a little bit older than me, maybe he was 30, named Terry.
We were chopping down weeds or something really physical on the hill.
We peeled off our shirts and our sweatshirts and our jackets, because we were getting hot, and threw them on the ground so we could get to the work with a vengeance.

Terry very carefully takes off his, he had a Zen style jacket, very carefully takes it off, folds it, doesn't immediately pick up his tools, sets it carefully down on the ground and says, "This is Buddha's clothing.
It's beautiful."
Never forgot that.
Once in a while, I notice a little more how wonderful it is to have clothing.
Because it's not just clothing, right?
So, to really appreciate everything.
And of course, hearing about war on the other side of the planet, also to appreciate safety.
Relative safety.
And then we hit the tough stuff here.
And here we probably hear the echoes of Shanti Deva, whom Chris loves and teaches often.
Tori Zenji is interested in how we can practice with difficult folks, including people who make wars.
*All the more we can be sympathetic and affectionate with foolish people, particularly with someone who becomes a sworn enemy and persecutes us with abusive language.
The very abuse conveys the Buddhist boundless, conveys the Buddhist boundless loving-kindness.
It is a compassionate device to liberate us entirely from the mean-spirited delusions we have built up with our wrongful conduct from the beginningless past.*
So this is pretty difficult, right?
How can we merge with confusion, with pain, with suffering?
And we see that as an opportunity for growth and learning and awakening, because, as he said earlier, everything is Buddha.
So even this, a simple answer.
And of course, the mind can argue all kinds of things about the importance of resisting, right?
Some things are not OK.
Precepts, right?
We have a tradition of strong ethical precepts, and yet somehow in our response to even violence, there is opportunity for liberation.
Somehow it's there, and your head's not so sure, but I think maybe the heart is like, yeah, yeah, maybe so.
And one simple thing I think of, and whatever I say about this kind of topic is a little too simplistic, but you have to say something: it's kind of like sustainable activism.
If the activism is rooted in anger and opposition and fighting, it does seem like people burn out.
But could activism be rooted in love and compassionate concern for the suffering of the oppressed and of the oppressor?
Thich Nhat Hanh, powerful model of that.
So we could think about him, maybe.
And then he goes on, and this section's really famous.
You see a lot of calligraphies and quotations of this next part.
*With our open response to such abuse, we completely relinquish ourselves, we let go.
And the most profound and pure faith arises.*
And this is the part:
*At the peak of each thought, a lotus flower opens.
And on each flower is revealed a Buddha.*
So imagine a little teeny Buddha sitting there, smiling.
*And everywhere is the pure land in its beauty.
We fully see the Tathagata's radiant light right where we are.
May we retain this mind and extend it throughout the world so that we and all beings become mature in Buddha's wisdom.*
So that's our hope, right?
Maturity, growing up as individuals, as a society, as a planet.
And it's so clear, right, that all the trouble, and one wants to say, well, most of the trouble, no, it's probably all the trouble comes from confused human minds.
Minds that are tangled by greed, hate, and delusion in all its many forms.
So here are these teachings that there's beauty there.
There's Buddha there.
That's what's meant by this great faith.
And it requires some great determination to put it into practice.
Great doubt, I'm going to set aside because it needs a lot of exploration.
The simple way to look at great doubt, which sounds like a bad thing, more or less, I think: what's great about doubt?
Faith, I can imagine, that's great, even if I don't like the word.
Determination, yeah, right, yeah.
Go.
But doubt.
I think a short version there is: don't be so sure.
That's one way to message or think about great doubt.
Don't be so sure that you know, right?
Who and what you are and how it all works.
Which is why we have practice, community, and teachings, right?
Because on some level we've recognized, I think, I kind of think, but no, I don't get it.
I tried to just figure it out.
But there's something wrong with that.
It's not quite working, right?
It's not quite complete.
There's suffering there.
So that's why we also have a tradition with such a warm human component, right?
Teacher, student, community, sangha, ancestors.
We help each other.
I've mostly had one teacher-student relationship.
Several of us have here, practicing all these years under Norman Fischer.
Who is, by the way, feeling much better.
I don't know if you've heard, he had a terrible bladder infection, and some of the prostate related issues that seem to be somewhat inevitable for older men.
But he got through it.
He's doing much better.
This was enough to keep Cathy, his wife, home.
She was going to come for our final sesshin the week before last, and I kept her home.

But anyway, he's doing much better, and he's looking forward to seeing us this June at our Samish Island seven day, eight night retreat, which you can register for now, thanks to Talus and Karen and others.
But anyway, I mostly have practiced with Norman all these years.
And for, you know, good, or sometimes it seems a little limiting maybe.
But wonderful.
But I've also had the good fortune to meet and be touched by several other teachers.
I guess you can hear the hesitation.
I have a little bit of self-guilt talk in there, like I should have reached out more, and I still can.
I'm still moving.
Practice more with other teachers.
So maybe I'll try to convert that little sense of not enough into letting it go, and also practice more with other teachers.
But anyway, one of them was Kyogen Carlson.
Kyogen and his wife Gyokuko, those are their Dharma names.
In their order you go exclusively by your Dharma name after ordination.

They did monastic practice together, full time, cloistered, stay out of the world, hardcore monastic practice for quite a few years, together at Shasta Abbey Buddhist Monastery in California on the slopes of Mount Shasta.
You can actually see the mountain really well from their property.
It's beautiful.
This monastery was founded by a powerful woman teacher named Jiyu-Kennett, who's worthy of much exploration and many talks.
Important ancestor.
She's a British woman who went to Japan in late middle age and took on the Japanese Zen establishment and said, "You're going to teach me.
I'm going to learn Zen from you."
And she really did.
She worked with a lot of cultural and sexist resistance there, anyway.
She was a great teacher and, of course, like all great teachers, had a lot of interesting quirks and problems.
And eventually she sent this couple, Kyogen and Gyokuko, from Mount Shasta to Portland.
Yes, that's the kind of organization that would send you somewhere, that kind of monasticism.
She sent them to Portland to create an abbey.
That's the language they use.
They use a more Christian language than some of the other groups.
To create an abbey in this lineage.
But things went south between them, and eventually Kyogen and Gyokuko broke off relations with their teacher.
It's the sad and difficult thing that does happen, for sure.
But they didn't stop.
They went on, and they probably did more than they would have done otherwise.
They went on to found an independent Soto Zen center called Dharma Rain Zen Center, which we've talked about on and off before.
I really recommend that if you're ever in Portland, you make a Portland weekend of it and go visit them.
It's a wonderful center and community.
They, I don't know, ten years ago maybe, audaciously purchased a large contaminated property in Portland, southeast Portland but within the city limits, kind of the edge.
This property was a brownfield used for freeway construction, where they dumped all the rubble and debris.
One doesn't really think about this after the freeway's already built, but an unbelievable amount of stuff got moved around to make that freeway be there, and a lot of it gets dumped somewhere.
So they had to cooperate with the EPA and state agencies and all kinds of stuff to gradually, little by little, start turning this brownfield, a big place, 10 to 12 acres, into a Zen center.
It's amazing.
Our modest ambition to think about trying to buy a little building for a Zen building feels modest in comparison, although that's challenging too.
Anyway, a little backstory on Kyogen.
That's why I mentioned all that.
Kyogen was a really wise, kind, thoughtful teacher, at least in my encounters with him, and I know some of his long-term students pretty well.

A story that comes to mind about him, from a couple of sesshin and seeing him at meetings: one time I was at a priest meeting, a Zen priest meeting, I think it might have been in Oregon somewhere, and I was hanging around with Kate and Michael, who are the teachers of the Mountain Rain Zen community.
This was some time ago.
Kate and Michael and I often talk shop, especially back then, and shop is sangha, right?
So we were talking about our confusion and challenges and how you make it all work, and different personalities, nothing disrespectful, of course, but, you know, like, "oh God."
Kyogen heard this and wandered over at the tea area, it was a coffee and tea area.
He heard us standing around with our coffee, and he listened for a while with a smile, and then he said, "Well, if zazen is in the middle of everything you do, it always works out.
It might not work out the way you think it will, but it always works out."
I was so amazed by that advice.
It really encouraged me and it still does.
So we try to keep zazen, keep meditation, in the middle.
We are all conditioned beings, whether we've been here for an hour or 20 years, with our confusions and desires and all the stuff.
But if zazen is in the middle, it should work out.
It's great.
So I want to share with you a little bit from Kyogen and then hear what you have to think about this great faith effort that I am dancing around a little bit.
One of Kyogen's students, Jiko Sallie Tisdale, put together a nice book of Kyogen's talks.
In his lifetime he published a small book, but after his death she published this.
Oh, his death is interesting too, and sad.
They were in the new, half-completed dharma hall they were building on this new property, so he lived to see the beginning.
And Sally Jiko, this woman who put this book together, was with him.
Maybe the foundation was poured or a little more, but Kyogen was very excited, pointing out where things were going to be and visualizing the space.
It must have been after early morning practice.
They went and had their oryoki breakfast together.
They really keep a formal residential practice.
Not a lot of full-time students, but there's always a few.
And then he was walking down the hall after breakfast and had a massive heart attack and was gone.
So that's how it can go, right?
Things happen suddenly.
Makes me think of you, of course, John.
Glad you're okay.
So here's a little from Kyogen Carlson about faith, about great faith.
*Faith has three aspects.
The first is the faith we need to engage in the practice.
In Zen Buddhist practice, what we call faith is a kind of an intuition.
An intuition.
We don't believe just in a story.
For us, faith is something different from a story.
It comes from the intuition that there is something to wake up to, something to do, something to find, something to know.
And when that intuition awakens, we call this way-seeking mind,* kind of a Zen gloss of the term bodhicitta, *way-seeking mind.
Once way-seeking mind appears, then the way appears.
It is possible to walk a path then.
We just know it must be so, but there's something to understand and it leads us to seek.*
So the first aspect of faith, he says, is the faith of practice, the faith of needing to practice.
*Second, our faith is that the Dharma wheel turns, that the Dharma functions.
And this is based on a simple observation that the Buddha made, that all beings want to avoid suffering, and all beings want to know ease.
It's the simplest observation in the world.
And because of it, karma tends towards enlightenment.
Because all beings want to be happy and know ease, don't want to suffer, karma tends towards enlightenment.
And as we refine what causes suffering, as we understand what causes suffering, we move away from samsara, the endlessly conditioned world of desires.
We become more ethical in our conduct, we care more about others, and because our own ease depends on this interconnection, this comes naturally.
Be more ethical, more caring.
We naturally move in this direction.
And the underlying principle of Dharma is this progression towards the good.*
So faith that we need to practice, a feeling of needing to practice, faith in the Dharma, we owe faith that it works in some organic natural way.
And then he says, the third, the deepest level of faith:
*No matter what happens, no matter how bad things are, way down at a fundamental level, it's okay.
Our faith comes down to this.
We know that this world will end.
We know that we ourselves will die.
We know our children will die.
We know the planet will die.
And what does this mean in the end?
When we relax very deeply into the thusness, into what truly is, there is peace, there is acceptance, and something on which we can rely.
This requires a very deep letting go.
When horrible things happen around us, I can let go.
I know I can let go.
Always I can rely on this.
And when I let go deeply into this vast thusness, it's okay.
Thusness, suchness, how it is.
And this is true for all beings, whether they know it or not.
Practicing faith on these three levels makes it possible to drop expectations in a really open-handed way.
Do you understand?
We know that it's okay, no matter what happens.
We can drop our particular expectations about events and be positive.
This is not surrender.
This is not resignation.
This is not bitterness.
It's just letting go.*
In the world of spirituality, this part's really interesting.
*In the world of spirituality, there's something I call the illusion of a key.
The illusion of a key, like a key and a lock.
The illusion is that there is a code to life, a code to the world.
If we just had that key, it would all make sense.
This illusion tells us that our suffering would go away when we figure it all out.
A lot of the storylines we add to religion have to do with this hope for a key.
Religion and lots of things.
I do believe that things beyond our comprehension do happen, and that they can be significant and meaningful.
But they don't explain everything.*
So not to think of big spiritual experiences as the key either, he says.
Though they can be significant and meaningful, they don't explain everything.
They don't give us a key.
Another path that I wanted to share, I think there was one, but I didn't mark it.
Oh yeah, I got this part.
*So faith is not about belief.
It has nothing to do with belief.
And knowing, for us, the knowing of Dharma, is also not about facts.
It's about answering the fundamental koan, the fundamental universal koan of how to be liberated without changing the external conditions at all.
How to be happy without arranging it all the way we want it.
Buddhism is not a religion of belief, but it is one of faith.
It takes faith to look for truth.
It takes faith to turn the mind towards the possible.
When we do this, we can be undefeated.
Unconquerable.
A spirit that's indomitable, no matter what.
We can keep our sanity as events unfold.
This is not faith in something external, something out there.
We don't have a savior.
Our way is the refuge of the three treasures.
We move from self to* what?
It says "from self to what?"
This is a big question.
*There's really nothing to hold.
At a point in one's practice, we go hurtling into the darkness.
It's like stepping off a cliff into a pitch black hole.
So we have to let ourselves do this.
Let ourselves fall without a point of reference.
Let things fall.
We have to let the self fall apart.
Our faith is in the process.
We have faith that others have done this.
That there's something here to awaken to.
Something that's not a something.
And there's a path in front of us.
Sometimes it's just a step, but it's all we need.
We take that one step, and the path opens up in front of us.*
The last little part about allowing ourselves to fall makes me think of an expression somebody shared with me from Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche, a fabulous, flawed teacher.
Trungpa Rinpoche said, "The bad news is we're all falling.
The good news is there's no bottom."
We can just keep falling.
Let ourselves fall.
So a few thoughts about great faith.
This point about the key is interesting, isn't it?
I notice, as I'm giving these talks, I want to know the key myself, and I want to share the key with you, and what's the key.
Especially this huge dynamic tension with something as horrible as war.
It's happening now, right?
And this idea of learning from and appreciating aggressors, that it all works out and we can let go.
It's not really something we can figure out, it seems.
But don't you feel, as I say that, and you contemplate that, and I'm sure you've contemplated this before, there's something there, right?
There's something important.
There's something that's worth continuing to seek and wonder about, feel into.
To notice when you try too hard in one direction or another, you get more unhappy.
When you just blow it off, you get more unhappy.
But where's that feeling of happiness and joy?
It's some kind of engagement that's soft, right?
Some kind of engagement that's open.
That's here.
That isn't trying to make things the way we want them exactly, while we're also serving with enthusiasm, doing what we can.
We say balance, but that's balance.
It's kind of like the idea of the key, right?
If there was one thing that was balanced, that's probably not true.
But still, we look for the key.
We look for balance.
And we keep practicing.
That's the faith thing.
Well, maybe I'll chant this out and turn off the recording, because I don't think you want to be on the recording.
And we'll see what comes to mind in some kind of response to all this.
*I can equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
The way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
